scenes.visual: Title card 'Where the Rain Falls' over a side-view cartoon globe, a green band at the equator and tan bands near 30 degrees north and south. COLOUR MAP, same in both films: RED line = monthly temperature; BLUE line = monthly rain; GOLD shading = a dry month; BLUE parcel = moist rising air; GOLD parcel = dry sinking air; GREEN = forest; TAN = desert or dry grass. Cream background, 16:9. Numbers appear only as on-screen text. Globes, parcels, trees and torches are simple cartoons labelled 'schematic'; climate-diagram lines and sunlight bars are computed from the lesson's numbers and labelled 'computed'.

scenes.tts: The Amazon and the Sahara are both hot. So why is one a rainforest, and the other a desert?
scenes.visual: Split screen: left, a dense green canopy labelled 'Amazon'; right, tan dunes labelled 'Sahara'. A thermometer icon slides between them and shows the same high reading on both sides; a question mark grows between the panels.
scenes.narration: The Amazon and the Sahara are both hot. So why is one a rainforest, and the other a desert?

scenes.tts: Each is a biome, a large region with similar climate and similar plants and animals. To guess a biome, ask two things of every month. How warm is it? How wet?
scenes.visual: The word 'biome' with a short definition card. Six small icons pop in a row: tropical wet forest, savanna, desert, temperate grassland, boreal forest, tundra. Then two empty boxes appear: a RED thermometer labelled 'warmth' and a BLUE raindrop labelled 'water', with 'each month' beneath.
scenes.narration: Each is a biome, a large region with similar climate and similar plants and animals. To guess a biome, ask two things of every month. How warm is it? How wet?

scenes.tts: Start with warmth. Shine a torch straight down at a table, and you get a small bright spot. Tilt it, and the same light spreads into a larger, dimmer oval.
scenes.visual: A cartoon torch above a table casts a small bright circle. The torch tilts; the circle stretches into a wide, dim oval while a counter of light rays stays the same (schematic).
scenes.narration: Start with warmth. Shine a torch straight down at a table, and you get a small bright spot. Tilt it, and the same light spreads into a larger, dimmer oval.

scenes.tts: Sunlight does the same on a round Earth. Averaged over a year, it strikes the equator most directly, and the poles at a slant. So the tropics get the most energy per square metre, and the poles the least.
scenes.visual: Parallel yellow rays hit the side-view globe: a tight bright patch at the equator, long dim patches near the poles (annual-average picture, schematic). Beside the globe a bar chart grows, computed annual-mean top-of-atmosphere sunlight: Equator 415, 30 N 365, 60 N 236, Pole 172 W per square metre (computed).
scenes.narration: Sunlight does the same on a round Earth. Averaged over a year, it strikes the equator most directly, and the poles at a slant. So the tropics get the most energy per square metre, and the poles the least.

scenes.tts: But the Amazon and the Sahara get similar average warmth. What differs is water, and moving air decides where it falls.
scenes.visual: The thermometer icon fades from both panels; the BLUE raindrop icon pulses beside the Amazon and is crossed out beside the Sahara. Arrows of air begin to stir above the globe.
scenes.narration: But the Amazon and the Sahara get similar average warmth. What differs is water, and moving air decides where it falls.

scenes.tts: Over the warm equator, moist air rises. As it rises, it expands and cools. Its water vapour condenses into cloud, and it rains. This is the equatorial rain belt.
scenes.visual: A BLUE parcel lifts off the equator of the globe, grows slightly larger as it climbs (expands), a small thermometer on it drops, a white cloud forms and blue rain streaks fall onto a GREEN band labelled 'equatorial rain belt'.
scenes.narration: Over the warm equator, moist air rises. As it rises, it expands and cools. Its water vapour condenses into cloud, and it rains. This is the equatorial rain belt.

scenes.tts: The air, now dry, flows toward the poles high up. Near thirty degrees north and south, it sinks back down.
scenes.caption: The air, now dry, flows toward the poles high up. Near 30° north and south, it sinks back down.
scenes.visual: The parcel, now pale, travels poleward high above the surface on both sides, then turns down near the 30 degree lines (labelled on screen). A closed loop arrow completes on each side of the equator.
scenes.narration: The air, now dry, flows toward the poles high up. Near 30° north and south, it sinks back down.

scenes.tts: Sinking air is squeezed, and it warms. Warming takes it further from the point where its vapour condenses. So sinking air stays clear, and rain is rare. Many great deserts lie beneath it, the Sahara among them.
scenes.visual: The descending parcel shrinks (compressed), its thermometer rises, and its colour shifts from pale blue to GOLD; its count of water-vapour dots stays the same. The sky beneath clears; the ground below fades from green to TAN. A tiny gauge labelled 'relative humidity' drops. Then TAN patches light up on a simple world outline near 30 degrees north and south; the Sahara is labelled.
scenes.narration: Sinking air is squeezed, and it warms. Warming takes it further from the point where its vapour condenses. So sinking air stays clear, and rain is rare. Many great deserts lie beneath it, the Sahara among them.

scenes.tts: So here is the first half of the rule. Rain falls where moist air rises and cools. It is scarce where air sinks and warms.
scenes.visual: Rule card builds in two lines: 'Rain where moist air rises and cools' (BLUE arrow up) and 'Scarce where air sinks and warms' (GOLD arrow down).
scenes.narration: So here is the first half of the rule. Rain falls where moist air rises and cools. It is scarce where air sinks and warms.

scenes.tts: The rain belt does not stay put. Through the year, it shifts north and south. It roughly follows the overhead Sun, but lags behind it.
scenes.visual: A small Sun icon marks the overhead point on the globe and slides north, then south, with month labels ticking past. The GREEN rain band and its cloud follow it with a visible lag, trailing a little behind the Sun icon rather than locked beneath it (schematic).
scenes.narration: The rain belt does not stay put. Through the year, it shifts north and south. It roughly follows the overhead Sun, but lags behind it.

scenes.tts: Picture a town some way north of the equator, near the edge of that swing. Does it get rain all year, or only part of it?
scenes.visual: A pin labelled 'a town some way north of the equator' sits on the globe near the northern edge of the band's swing. The rain band hovers over it, then begins to slide away. Large on-screen question: 'Rain all year, or only part?'
scenes.narration: Picture a town some way north of the equator, near the edge of that swing. Does it get rain all year, or only part of it?

scenes.visual: Hold on the pin and the frozen rain band; a small timer ring fills over five seconds.

scenes.tts: Only part of it. The town is wet while the rain belt is overhead, and dry when the belt moves away. A wet season, then a dry one.
scenes.visual: The band slides over the pin (cloud, rain, label 'wet season'), then away (clear sky, label 'dry season'). A twelve-month strip under the pin fills BLUE for the wet months and GOLD for the dry months (schematic).
scenes.narration: Only part of it. The town is wet while the rain belt is overhead, and dry when the belt moves away. A wet season, then a dry one.

scenes.tts: Ecologists draw that on a climate diagram. Months run along the bottom. A red line shows temperature. A blue line shows rain.
scenes.visual: The twelve-month strip unrolls into an empty chart: months J to D on the x axis, a RED temperature line and a BLUE rain line draw in from left to right (schematic shapes).
scenes.narration: Ecologists draw that on a climate diagram. Months run along the bottom. A red line shows temperature. A blue line shows rain.

scenes.tts: The scales are linked, so ten degrees sits level with twenty millimetres. When the blue line drops below the red, the month is read as dry.
scenes.caption: The scales are linked, so 10 °C sits level with 20 mm. When the blue line drops below the red, the month is read as dry.
scenes.visual: Two axes light up: left 'temperature, degrees C', right 'rain, mm', with tick 10 beside tick 20 joined by a dashed line. Where the BLUE line dips under the RED one, the gap fills GOLD and a label reads 'dry month: rain (mm) < 2 x temperature (degrees C)'.
scenes.narration: The scales are linked, so 10 °C sits level with 20 mm. When the blue line drops below the red, the month is read as dry.

scenes.tts: That is the second half of the rule. The warmer a month, the more rain it needs to count as humid.
scenes.visual: The RED line slides upward; the GOLD dry region widens beneath it even though the BLUE line has not moved. Rule card adds a third line: 'Warmer months need more rain'.
scenes.narration: That is the second half of the rule. The warmer a month, the more rain it needs to count as humid.

scenes.tts: Read month by month, warmth and water give a first guess at the biome. A guess, not a final answer.
scenes.visual: The diagram shrinks beside the globe; a GREEN forest icon and a TAN desert icon attach to matching diagrams, each with a small label 'first guess'.
scenes.narration: Read month by month, warmth and water give a first guess at the biome. A guess, not a final answer.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'Rain follows rising moist air; warmer months need more of it.'
